title: How your phone screen knows exactly where you touched
description: Your screen doesn't sense pressure. It senses your finger's effect on an electric field. Here's how that becomes a tap.

scenes.big: How a screen finds your finger
scenes.say: Your phone screen doesn't feel pressure. It feels electricity. Here's how it finds your finger.

steps: Grid of clear electrodes under glass
Chip measures the field at each crossing
Your finger disturbs the field nearby
Biggest change marks the touch point
scenes.say: Under the glass is a grid of transparent electrodes, in rows and columns. A chip measures the electric field at every crossing. Your finger conducts, so it disturbs the field and changes the capacitance there. The spot with the change is where you touched.

Most phones use mutual capacitance, which measures the coupling between each pair of crossing electrodes. Because every crossing is read separately, the screen can track several fingers at once. That's what makes pinch-to-zoom possible.
It has limits, though. Direct contact matters. Water and smudges can confuse the grid, which is why a wet screen sometimes acts possessed.
Each report is just coordinates. Software turns them into taps, swipes and pinches. Follow for more everyday tech, decoded.
